title: A Lens Passing By
subtitle: Microlensing light curves, and what one curve cannot tell you
body:
Step 1 of 10 read

A star brightens and fades

When a lens passes almost in front of a star, the two images are too close together to resolve (a milliarcsecond apart), but together they carry more light than the star alone. The star brightens and fades again as the lens moves on, for days or weeks.

The instrument draws the light curve: flux over its quiet baseline against time. It depends on how close the pass is (u0, in Einstein radii) and on the crossing time tE the lens takes to move one Einstein radius, which in turn depends on the lens's mass, distance and speed. This is a model: one point lens moving in a straight line past one star.

title: A Lens Passing By
subtitle: Microlensing light curves, and what one curve cannot tell you
body:
Step 10 of 10 read

What you worked out

A lens passing in front of a star brightens it by (u² + 2) ÷ (u √(u² + 4)), 10 for a pass at a tenth of the Einstein radius, over a crossing time of weeks for a star-mass lens. The curve fixes that time but not the mass, the distance and the speed that made it. Blended light lowers the peak, and a finite star caps it. In the advanced depth you fit a synthetic event and see how an assumption about the blend changes the answer.
